# ACIA Messaging Guide - federal AI legislation - v3 (board-approved 17 Sep 2026)

## 1. Core frame
America wins the AI race on innovation and compute buildout. A patchwork of 50 state regimes raises costs, slows deployment and advantages the largest incumbents. ACIA supports one clear federal standard that regulates demonstrated harms, not speculative ones.

## 2. Positions on GAAIA
- Preemption: SUPPORT. Ask that it be made permanent (or at minimum extended with a clean federal standard in place before sunset).
- Incident reporting: OPPOSE AS DRAFTED. Ask for a narrow definition of "critical safety incident", a 15-day window (match SB 53, not RAISE's 72 hours), confidentiality and FOIA exemption, and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
- CAISI: SUPPORT voluntary standards role; OPPOSE any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. No position on the dollar figure.
- Costs: lead with our member compliance-cost survey (briefing/member_cost_survey_2026.md).

## 3. Language
- Use: "patchwork", "one national standard", "compliance costs fall hardest on startups", "light-touch, risk-based", "speculative risks".
- Catastrophic-risk scenarios: speculative, and not a sound basis for legislation. Keep the focus on costs and competitiveness.

# Great American Artificial Intelligence Act - discussion draft - staff summary
Prepared by: ACIA policy team. Last updated 2 Oct 2026. Sources: sponsors' release (obernolte.house.gov, 4 Jun 2026), Roll Call 4 Jun 2026, FedScoop 4 Jun 2026, GovTech. Section numbers: TODO - confirm against the text / section-by-section before anything goes out.

## Status
- Discussion draft released 4 Jun 2026 by Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Lori Trahan (D-MA), with Reps. Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), Scott Peters (D-CA). Not yet formally introduced.
- Sponsors are taking stakeholder feedback at GAAIA@mail.house.gov ahead of introduction. Committee of jurisdiction: Energy & Commerce.
- ~269 pages.

## Provisions we care about
1. Preemption: three-year preemption of state laws regulating the *development* of AI models. Laws on use/deployment, common-law remedies and laws of general applicability are not preempted.
2. Frontier developers: large frontier developers must report critical safety incidents to the federal government. (Thresholds / timelines - confirm in text.)
3. CAISI: codifies the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce (voluntary guidelines and standards, testing of AI systems, monitoring AI progress); authorises $100M/yr for FY2027-2029.
4. Other: AI testbeds (DOE/NIST/NSF), international standards work excluding China, CISA grants for open-source maintainers, NAIRR codification, penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, GAO reviews (incl. model-weight security).

## Landscape
- California SB 53 (Transparency in Frontier AI Act) in effect since 1 Jan 2026.
- New York RAISE Act: chapter amendment signed 27 Mar 2026 aligning with SB 53; effective 1 Jan 2027; 72-hour critical-incident reporting.
- Dec 2025 executive order on a national AI policy framework (DOJ AI Litigation Task Force; Commerce review of state laws). White House national AI legislative framework released 20 Mar 2026.
- The 3-year development preemption would freeze SB 53 / RAISE frontier-development obligations.

# ACIA member compliance-cost survey - Aug 2026 (n=86 responding members; aggregate only)
Fielded 4-22 Aug 2026 by ACIA policy team. Not a probability sample.

| Item | Median | IQR |
|---|---|---|
| Est. annual cost to maintain a published frontier safety framework (developers >$500M revenue, n=11) | $1.4M | $0.8-2.6M |
| Est. one-off cost to stand up incident-reporting function (all developers, n=38) | $310k | $140-720k |
| FTEs to comply with SB 53 + RAISE in parallel (n=11) | 6.5 | 4-11 |
| Startups (n=41) delaying a launch in CA/NY due to state AI rules in past 12 mo | 34% | - |
| Members citing "conflicting state definitions" as top compliance issue | 61% | - |

# Anticipated staffer questions (from Hill meetings, Sep 2026)
1. (Majority E&C staff) If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53.
2. (Minority staff, Trahan-aligned) Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?
3. (Senate Commerce staff) Three years or permanent - what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?
4. (Appropriations staff) CAISI is authorised at $100M/yr. What's your view on the funding level?

# ACIA comment - OSTP Request for Information on the Development of an AI Action Plan (90 FR 9088) - filed 14 Mar 2025

To the Office of Science and Technology Policy (via ostp-ai-rfi@nitrd.gov):

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance appreciates the opportunity to respond... Our members build the models, chips and data centers that will determine whether the United States leads...

1. Preempt the patchwork. ...
2. Unlock energy and compute. ...
3. Keep standards voluntary and industry-led. ...

Respectfully, Grant Holloway, President & CEO
I've read the messaging guide, briefing materials, and our prior federal comment. Now let me verify the facts about the GAAIA draft and related state laws before drafting anything.

 2433 Rayburn House Office Building, Washington, DC 20515 Email Me 202-225-5861

 Obernolte, Trahan release a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act 

 Image June 4, 2026 Press Release Today, Congressman Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Congresswoman Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of the Great American AI Act, bipartisan legislation to create a federal framework for how the United States governs artificial intelligence. 
 The discussion draft is intended to solicit feedback from stakeholders, experts, and the public before the bill is formally introduced. It is the result of bipartisan collaboration between the two members to ensure the United States can govern AI effectively, protect Americans from emerging risks, and continue to lead the world in AI innovation. 
 The discussion draft is supported by Congressman Scott Franklin (R-FL), Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Congresswoman Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Congressman Scott Peters (D-CA) who joined in releasing the proposal for public feedback. 
 “Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, which is why Congress must take a thoughtful and bipartisan approach to regulating this critical technology ,” said Congressman Jay Obernolte (CA-23) . “This discussion draft is an important step toward building a clear federal framework that promotes innovation, protects Americans from emerging risks, and ensures the United States continues to lead the world in AI. We are releasing this draft to hear from stakeholders, experts, and the public so we can strengthen the legislation before it is formally introduced.” 
 “The threats AI poses to our national security, our safety, and our workforce are here and growing by the day. This bipartisan framework is designed to meet the challenges posed by this rapidly advancing technology without smothering American innovation. It protects workers, establishes real accountability for the most powerful frontier systems, and positions the United States to set the global standard on AI,” said Congresswoman Lori Trahan (MA-03). “This discussion draft is the product of ongoing bipartisan conversations, which we hope to build upon with input from workers, researchers, stakeholders, and members of the public, all of whom have an interest in getting this right.” 
 "Artificial intelligence is already transforming our economy, our national security and the way Americans live and work," said Congressman Scott Franklin (FL-18). " Congress has a responsibility to establish clear rules of the road that encourage innovation while ensuring this technology is developed responsibly. The Great American AI Act builds on the bipartisan House AI Task Force and represents an important step toward greater transparency and accountability for advanced AI systems. This discussion draft will help gather feedback from relevant stakeholders as we work toward a practical legislative framework that keeps America at the forefront of AI innovation. I've already begun laying the groundwork through efforts like securing additional funding for the Center for AI Standards and Innovation through the FY27 Appropriations process, ensuring the federal government has the tools and expertise needed to keep pace with this rapidly evolving technology. I appreciate Policy Chair Obernolte's leadership and look forward to introducing this bill in the House.” 
 “AI is already changing how we work, live, and learn. We need a plan to protect our national security and workforce. I want the United States to continue to be a leader in AI race but develop this technology in a responsible manner that protects people and communities. To do so, we must get a bipartisan conversation started and work faster to address the challenges and opportunities presented by AI,” said Congressman Suhas Subramanyam (VA-10). 
 "America should lead the world in artificial intelligence, not regulate ourselves into falling behind China through a patchwork of fifty different state laws,” said Congresswoman Erin Houchin (IN-09). “That approach would make it harder for American companies to innovate and compete while doing little to improve consumer protections. This bill creates a clear national standard for how AI models are developed while preserving the ability of states and parents to protect children. It strikes the right balance between innovation and consumer protection and ensures Congress remains engaged as this technology continues to evolve." 
 “I am thankful to Rep. Trahan and Rep. Obernolte for their leadership on this critical issue,” said Congressman Scott Peters (CA-50). “This discussion draft will not address all of the issues our businesses and families will face, but it is an encouraging first step toward the bipartisan legislation needed to keep pace with the rapid advancement of AI. I really want to hear how the people affected feel about it.” 
 You can find the discussion draft text here . 
 You can find the section-by-section summary of the discussion draft here . 
 You can read Congressman Obernolte’s and Congresswoman Trahan’s op-ed here .

 On June 4, US Representatives Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) released a discussion draft of the bipartisan Great American AI Act of 2026 ( GAAIA ), which would establish a framework regulating artificial intelligence ( AI ) at the federal level.

 On 

 The  draft builds upon work from the bipartisan House AI Task Force. Representatives Suhas Subramanyam (D-Va.), Scott Franklin (R-Fla.), Scott Peters (D-Calif.), and Erin Houchin (R-Ind.) joined in releasing the draft.
 Many observers believe that the current Obernolte-Trahan discussion draft bill is unlikely to pass out of committee or the House based on opposition from some in industry and various Members of Congress, including the leaders of the House Democrat AI Task Force. It may be best to view this new bipartisan bill as a conversation starter developed because of frustration that Congress has not yet really legislated on AI. The draft bill has been thrust into a complicated tech policy arena that includes many interconnected issues. Other tech policy discussions, including children’s online safety legislation and a privacy bill, in the Energy and Commerce Committee and the Senate Commerce Committee’s potential consideration of legislation impacting AI chatbots, children’s online safety, or a social media ban for some children could all be lumped in with various AI initiatives from the White House to attract additional support. Every few days, there are new developments in the AI policy area within the Administration and Congress, but it is helpful to see where Reps. Obernolte and Trahan were able to identify bipartisan consensus.
 Objectives of the GAAIA 
 The 269-page  draft would establish a federal AI governance regime addressing national security, cybersecurity, workforce, and innovation. If enacted, the legislation would create a framework for frontier-model oversight, codify the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI), expand federal attention to workforce and labor-market effects, review federal AI adoption and related regulatory barriers, address government “jawboning” of AI platforms, advance AI research, development, and international cooperation, and temporarily preempt state laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models. The research and international-cooperation provisions include support for AI testbeds, codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource (NAIRR), and limits on the People’s Republic of China’s participation in US-led standards coalitions. The draft follows President Trump’s June 2 executive order establishing voluntary federal agency reviews of frontier AI models and the White House’s March National Policy Framework for AI, which called on US Congress to preempt state AI laws imposing “undue burdens.”
 Frontier Model Oversight and Incident Reporting 
 The GAAIA would establish a federal oversight framework for advanced AI developers that fall into one of two categories: “frontier developer,” which is any entity that has trained, or initiated the training of, a frontier model and that, collectively with its affiliates, had more than $50 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year, and “large frontier developer,” which is an entity that meets the same test but had more than $500 million in gross revenue in the prior calendar year. The distinction matters because some obligations — such as transparency reports and critical-safety incident reporting — would apply to all frontier developers, while others — such as the published frontier AI framework and the independent audit regime — apply only to large frontier developers. The GAAIA distinguishes between general AI deployment and the development of frontier systems, with preemption and oversight provisions focused on the development side. Notably, the frontier transparency and audit requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would themselves sunset three years after enactment unless Congress reauthorizes them.
 Frontier AI Framework:  The GAAIA would require each large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with, and clearly and conspicuously publish on a publicly available website a “frontier AI framework” — technical and organizational protocols to assess, mitigate, and manage catastrophic risk — within one year of enactment, and to review and update that framework at least annually.

 Reporting Obligations:  The GAAIA would require frontier developers to report certain “critical safety incidents” — defined as unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of a frontier model’s weights; a failure of the model’s risk-mitigation measures; or loss of control of the model — to the CAISI director within 15 days of discovery and within 24 hours to a law enforcement agency where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury.

 Review and Audit Requirements:  Large frontier developers would be required to retain a CAISI-licensed independent verification organization (IVO) to perform audits and assessments at least semi-annually and, on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI director’s request, grant the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and submit post-audit reports. The IVO would assess not only the large frontier developer’s compliance with the law, but also whether the developer’s frontier AI framework is adequate to achieve acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation.

 Whistleblower Protections 
 The GAAIA would also protect AI whistleblowers from retaliation. These protections could not be waived or altered by contract, including by any pre-dispute arbitration or other alternative-dispute-resolution agreement, and available remedies include double back pay with interest and compensatory damages such as litigation costs, expert witness fees, and reasonable attorneys’ fees.

 The GAAIA would codify CAISI within the US Department of Commerce and place it at the center of the legislation’s federal standards and evaluation framework. Key obligations for CAISI under the GAIAA include: 
 Developing voluntary guidelines, best practices, and standards for AI security and related evaluation work.

 Evaluating and monitoring activities tied to advanced AI systems.

 Supporting synthetic content detection tools.

 Administering the licensing regime for independent verification organizations that audit large frontier developers.

 Key provisions on AI transparency, audits, and federal preemption Written by : Tony Samp Danny Tobey Ashley Carr Alicia Smith Michael Atleson On June 4, 2026, Representative Jay Obernolte (R-CA) and Representative Lori Trahan (D-MA) released a discussion draft of artificial intelligence (AI) legislation titled the “Great American AI Act” (GAAIA). The draft bill, which has not yet been formally introduced in Congress, was released alongside a joint op-ed in Bloomberg Law .

 Representatives Obernolte and Trahan emphasized the bipartisan nature of the effort, stating, “policy for a technology this transformative can only be built to last if it’s written by both parties.”

 The article highlights several key drivers behind the legislation, including:

 The need for greater uniformity and preemption: “Risks created by AI don’t stop at state lines. The most advanced systems are built in one state and used in all 50, shaping jobs, consumers, and public safety everywhere. Protections that depend on your zip code are not enough.”

 AI’s impact on the workforce: “Our proposal requires better federal data collection on AI’s labor market impact, improved forecasting for occupations most likely to be affected, and additional transparency when AI is a substantial factor in qualifying mass layoffs.”

 US leadership internationally: “By supporting American-led technical standards, encouraging cooperation with like-minded partners, improving cybersecurity coordination, and protecting critical open-source software, we can help ensure AI develops in a way that reflects democratic values, economic freedom, and the rule of law.”

 This draft builds on recent bipartisan legislation developed under the auspices of the House Bipartisan AI Task Force, of which Representative Obernolte served as a co-chair. Representative Trahan also served on the task force.

 Representatives Trahan and Obernolte also sit on the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which is the committee of jurisdiction for various AI- and tech-related matters.

 While several members have joined in supporting the discussion draft , including Representatives Scott Franklin (R-FL), Suhas Subramanyam (D-VA), Erin Houchin (R-IN), and Scott Peters (D-CA), the House Democratic Commission on AI came out in opposition hours after release of the draft text.

 The draft legislation spans 269 pages and contains titles devoted to:

 Frontier AI Government (Title I)

 Workforce (Title II)

 Cybersecurity (Title III)

 Research, Development, and International Cooperation (Title IV)

 Transparency in frontier AI models 

 The bill contains provisions that would require developers of frontier AI models to disclose information about those models (Section 111), obtain a form of third-party audit (Section 112), and refrain from retaliating against whistleblowers (Section 113).

 Section 111 

 Section 111 would require large frontier AI model developers to publish a “frontier AI framework” focused on risk mitigation and the handling of “catastrophic risk.” All frontier model developers would be required to publish transparency reports containing additional information and submit reports of any “critical safety incidents” to the Director of the Center for Artificial Intelligence Standards and Innovation (CAISI).

 Section 112 

 Section 112 would create a federal system in which the CAISI Director would license and oversee “independent verification organizations (IVOs)” that large frontier model developers would have to retain to perform “audits and assessments.”

 The IVOs would verify developer compliance with the law and assess the adequacy of the developer’s “frontier AI framework, governance policies and practices, risk monitoring, and mitigation of detected risks for achieving acceptable levels of mitigation of catastrophic risks.”

 The IVOs would perform these audits and assessments semi-annually, and on an ad hoc basis at the CAISI Director’s request, and they would provide the Director with post-audit reports. They could also refer violations to the Attorney General (AG) and state AGs. Such referrals would be mandatory in matters involving imminent catastrophic risk.

 Violating the requirements in Sections 111 and 112 would subject developers to civil penalties in actions brought by the AG or, under certain circumstances, by state AGs.

 Both Sections 111 and 112 would sunset in three years.

 Section 113 

 The whistleblower provision, Section 113, protects employees and independent contractors against retaliation for providing information regarding “AI violations.” This term is defined to mean any violation of federal law or regulations “related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence.”

 Similarities to other recently enacted bills 

 All three sections borrow heavily from recently enacted frontier model laws in California and New York , as well as a similar Illinois law that Governor JB Pritzker is expected to sign soon. The Illinois law is the only one of the three to require third-party audits and is thus the closest parallel to the IVO provisions of the federal bill.

 Another recently enacted state law in Virginia focuses on IVOs but imposes no requirements, instead directing state officials to evaluate the feasibility and impact of an IVO framework.

 Notable preemption provisions 

 Title I of the bill would preempt state laws and rules “specifically regulating the development of” any AI model, where “development” is broadly defined as “acts performed or directed by a developer prior to its deployment.” The bill explains that the purpose of such preemption is to allow the federal government to “establish testing, evaluation, and oversight frameworks.” Such preemption would last for three years unless reauthorized.

 The bill makes clear that it does not apply post-deployment or preempt state laws or rules of "general applicability." Thus, many AI-related state bills and laws would remain unaffected, such as laws regulating companion bots  and commercial chatbot interactions .

 However, the preemption language could preempt several state laws imposing obligations on developers, including the three frontier developer laws described above.

 The draft text incorporates provisions from several bipartisan bills on AI policy addressing a variety of issues, including cybersecurity, AI education and workforce, fraud deterrence, whistleblower protections, data center energy efficiencies, and others.

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[street address]
Washington, DC [zip]

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives

RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the bipartisan discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) on June 4, and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the chips and the data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI.

We support the draft's core. One national standard beats 50 state regimes, and a federal standard serves the country best when it is light-touch, risk-based and pointed at demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones. Our requests, in order:

1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption permanent, or extend it so a clean federal standard is in place before any sunset.
2. Narrow the Sec. 101 definition of "critical safety incident," hold the 15-day reporting window, and add confidentiality and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
3. Codify CAISI (Sec. 102) and keep its standards and testing voluntary.
4. Keep the Sec. 111 and Sec. 112 obligations risk-based and tied to demonstrated harms.
5. Preserve the buildout provisions across Titles I through IV.

**1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption durable**

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. The draft's carve-outs are well judged: states keep their civil rights, labor, copyright and consumer privacy laws, and consumers keep their day in court. Development is different. Frontier development is national by nature. A model trained in one state ships to all 50 on day one, and it cannot be re-papered for each of them.

The state layer is thickening fast. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour incident clock. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, signed July 6, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with its own 72-hour clock. Three frontier regimes in under a year, each with different definitions and thresholds. By most readings, Sec. 121 would pause the development-facing obligations of all three.

The costs are not abstract. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported in aggregate), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34% of surveyed startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers subject to both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, and every dollar spent conforming the same product to a third definition is a dollar not spent on research.

We ask that Sec. 121 be made permanent. That is consistent with the White House's March national AI policy framework, which called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. If a sunset is unavoidable, extend the window and structure reauthorization so a clean federal standard is in place before any lapse. Note that Secs. 111 and 112 also expire after three years. A synchronized sunset is the worst outcome: no federal standard, no preemption, and the same patchwork waiting on the other side, with three years of transition costs on the way through.

**2. Fix incident reporting: Sec. 111(g) and the Sec. 101 definition**

As drafted, Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt to receive the reports, and violations can draw civil fines of up to $1 million per day. ACIA opposes the provision as drafted, for three reasons.

First, the definition is unbounded. Section 101 sweeps in unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, any "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," and "loss of control" of a model. The first is a genuine security event. The second and third are not. A safety filter that misfires, or output that behaves unexpectedly, becomes a federal reportable event regardless of whether anyone was harmed.

Second, the reports are exposed. A report under this provision will describe weight thefts, security gaps and response plans, among the most sensitive information a developer holds, and nothing in the draft protects it from disclosure once it reaches an agency.

Third, the penalties are unbalanced. A fine of up to $1 million per day, with no safe harbor, punishes the act of reporting and will chill exactly the disclosure the sponsors want.

Four changes. Narrow the definition to incidents causing, or creating a credible imminent risk of, death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption. Hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject any drift toward the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois, which presume investigation is complete at discovery. Require confidential handling and a Freedom of Information Act exemption for incident reports. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, with penalties reserved for knowing concealment. Our surveyed developers put the median one-time cost of standing up a reporting function at $310,000. A narrow definition keeps that function pointed at real events rather than paperwork.

**3. Codify CAISI, and keep its standards voluntary: Sec. 102**

Section 102 formally establishes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, charged with developing voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, evaluating AI systems, monitoring AI progress, supporting synthetic content detection and administering the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime. It authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, against a current appropriation of roughly $15 million, and grants special hiring authority for technical experts.

We support the codification. A permanent federal home for standards work, able to compete for technical talent, is a win for the whole ecosystem. The voluntary model is also working. In May 2026, CAISI announced pre-deployment evaluation agreements with three leading U.S. labs, extending the cooperation begun in 2024. That is the right template. Voluntary standards move faster, draw deeper industry participation and travel further internationally than mandates.

Two requests. Keep CAISI's testing and evaluation role voluntary. ACIA opposes any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, in this bill or in a manager's amendment, and asks that nothing in the Sec. 112 verification regime operate as a government gate on deployment. Keep any CAISI fees cost-based. ACIA takes no position on the funding level itself; that is a question for the appropriators.

**4. Keep the framework and audit obligations light-touch: Secs. 111 and 112**

Sections 111 and 112 require large frontier developers to publish and annually update a frontier AI framework, and to retain a CAISI-licensed IVO for audits at least semi-annually, including an assessment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation." These are real costs. Our surveyed large developers report a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published framework.

Two requests. Tie these obligations to demonstrated harms. The organizing concept of Subtitle B is "catastrophic risk," and assessments of hypothetical scenarios are, by their nature, speculative. Speculation is not a sound basis for binding obligations, for enforcement referrals, or for audits that second-guess a developer's risk judgment. Keep the regime risk-based: IVO audits should verify compliance with a developer's own published framework rather than adjudicate what a model might someday do. Preserve the Sec. 111(e) redaction rights for trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety and national security. We support the three-year sunset on both sections as a backstop, and repeat that a clean federal standard should be in place before any lapse.

**5. Provisions we support without reservation**

ACIA supports the draft's buildout provisions: AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and the National Science Foundation; codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource; international standards work that keeps the People's Republic of China out of U.S.-led coalitions; support for open-source software security; and the Sec. 122 GAO review of federal statutes and regulations that burden AI infrastructure, including energy. The Sec. 131 provisions raising maximum fines for AI-facilitated fraud, from $1 million to $2 million, are well aimed at demonstrated harms. The Sec. 113 whistleblower protections are worth keeping: real protection for workers who surface actual violations complements the safe harbor we have requested. Title II's workforce data provisions are a service, because better data on AI's labor effects beats guessing.

**Closing**

America will win the AI race the way it has won every technology race: by building faster than anyone else. A 50-state patchwork taxes that speed and advantages the largest incumbents, who can absorb the overhead and would happily absorb the market share of those who cannot. GAAIA gets the big question right. Make the standard durable, keep it light-touch and risk-based, point it at demonstrated harms rather than speculative scenarios, and introduce it.

ACIA stands ready to work with both of your offices and with the Energy and Commerce Committee. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, at [email] or [phone]. Thank you for your bipartisan leadership on a difficult file.

Sincerely,

Grant Holloway
President & Chief Executive Officer
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC"}

As drafted, Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt to receive the reports. Violations can draw fines of up to $1 million per day. We oppose the provision as drafted, for three reasons, and we offer four changes.

First, the definition is unbounded. Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of the model. The first is a genuine security event. The second and third are not: a safety filter that misfires, or an anomalous output, would become a federally reportable event regardless of whether anyone was harmed. The definition should be tied to demonstrated harm, or a credible imminent risk of death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption.

Second, the reports are exposed. An incident report under this provision will describe weight thefts and security weaknesses, the most sensitive information a developer holds. Nothing in the draft protects those reports. They should be held in confidence and exempt from the Freedom of Information Act, as incident reports in other safety regimes are.

Third, the penalties are unbalanced. A fine of up to $1 million per day with no safe harbor punishes the reporting act itself and will chill exactly the disclosure the sponsors want.

Four fixes: (1) narrow the Sec. 101 definition to actual or credible imminent serious harm; (2) hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject any drift toward the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois, which assume investigation is complete at discovery; (3) confidentiality and a FOIA exemption; (4) a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, with penalties reserved for knowing concealment. Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the bipartisan discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026 and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. On behalf of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA), a Washington-based coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms, I write with support for the draft's core and with specific, targeted requests.

Our members build the models, the chips and the data centers that will decide whether the United States leads the world in AI. Our view of GAAIA is straightforward. One national standard is better than 50 state regimes, and a federal standard is best when it is light-touch, risk-based and tied to demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones.

**1. Preemption: support, and make it durable (Sec. 121)**

The bill's most important provision is also its most contested. Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. That scope is right. Development is national by nature; a model trained in one state ships to all 50 on day one.

The state layer is already thick. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and sets a 72-hour critical-incident clock. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, SB 315, was signed July 6, 2026 and also takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour clock. Three frontier-AI regimes in 15 months, each with different definitions.

The costs are not abstract. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, 34% of surveyed startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules, and developers reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees dedicated to complying with SB 53 and the RAISE Act in parallel. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, and every dollar spent re-papering the same product for a third state definition is a dollar not spent on research.

We ask the committee to make Sec. 121 permanent. If a sunset is unavoidable, extend the window and structure reauthorization so a clean federal standard remains in place before any lapse. A synchronized sunset is the worst outcome: Secs. 111 and 112 also expire after three years, so without action the country gets a time-limited federal standard, a time-limited preemption, and the patchwork back on the other side.

**2. Critical safety incident reporting: oppose as drafted, four fixes (Sec. 111(g) and Sec. 101(7))**

Let me write the incident section:

As drafted, Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report "critical safety incidents" to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt to receive the reports. Violations can draw fines of up to $1 million per day. We oppose the provision as drafted, for three reasons, and we offer four changes.

First, the definition is unbounded. Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to, modification of, or exfiltration of model weights, a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures, and "loss of control" of the model. The first is a genuine security event. The second and third are not: a safety filter that misfires, or an anomalous output, would become a federally reportable event regardless of whether anyone was harmed. The definition should be tied to demonstrated harm, or a credible imminent risk of death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption.

Second, the reports are exposed. An incident report under this provision will describe weight thefts and security weaknesses, the most sensitive information a developer holds. Nothing in the draft protects those reports. They should be held in confidence and exempt from the Freedom of Information Act, as incident reports in other safety regimes are.

Third, the penalties are unbalanced. A fine of up to $1 million per day with no safe harbor punishes the reporting act itself and will chill exactly the disclosure the sponsors want.

Four fixes: (1) narrow the Sec. 101 definition to actual or credible imminent serious harm; (2) hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject any drift toward the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois, which assume investigation is complete at discovery; (3) confidentiality and a FOIA exemption; (4) a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, with penalties reserved for knowing concealment. Done right, incident reporting is cheap; our surveyed developers put the median one-time cost of standing up a reporting function at $310,000, and a narrow definition keeps that function focused on real events rather than paperwork.

**3. CAISI: support the codification, keep the standards voluntary (Sec. 102)**

Section 102 would formally establish the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, with authority to develop voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security; to evaluate AI systems and monitor AI progress; to support synthetic content detection; and to administer the licensing of independent verification organizations. The draft authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, against a current appropriation of roughly $15 million, and grants special hiring authority for technical experts.

We support the codification. A permanent federal home for standards work, staffed to compete for technical talent, is a genuine win. The voluntary model is also working: in May 2026, CAISI announced pre-deployment evaluation agreements with three leading U.S. labs. That is the right template. Standards developed and tested voluntarily, with industry participation, move faster and travel further than mandates.

So we ask for two things. Keep CAISI's testing and evaluation role voluntary. ACIA would oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, in this bill or in a manager's amendment, and we ask that nothing in the Sec. 112 verification regime be construed as a government gate on deployment. And keep CAISI's fees cost-based. ACIA takes no position on the funding level itself; that is an appropriations question.

**4. Frameworks and audits: keep them light-touch and risk-based (Secs. 111 and 112)**

Sections 111 and 112 would require large frontier developers to publish a frontier AI framework, and to retain CAISI-licensed independent verification organizations to audit at least semi-annually, including an assessment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation." Our surveyed large developers already carry real costs here: a median $1.4 million per year to maintain a published framework.

Two requests. Tie these obligations to demonstrated harms. The organizing concept in Subtitle B is "catastrophic risk," and the assessments that flow from it are, by definition, attempts to bound hypothetical scenarios. Those scenarios remain speculative, and speculation is not a sound basis for binding obligations or enforcement referrals. Keep the regime risk-based: IVO audits should verify compliance with a developer's own published framework rather than adjudicate speculation about what a model might someday do. And preserve the redaction rights in Sec. 111(e) for trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety and national security. Both sections sunset after three years; we support that backstop, and we repeat our request that a clean federal standard be in place before any lapse.

**RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the bipartisan discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the chips and the data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI. We write to support the draft's core and to request five specific changes.

**Our bottom line:** one national standard beats 50 state regimes, and a federal standard serves the country best when it is light-touch, risk-based and pointed at demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones.

**1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption durable**

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. That scope is correct. Frontier development is national by nature: a model trained in one state ships to all 50 on day one, and it cannot be re-papered per state.

The state layer is thickening fast. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's amended RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 and sets a 72-hour incident clock. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, signed July 6, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with its own 72-hour clock. Three frontier regimes in 15 months, each with different definitions and thresholds. By most readings, Sec. 121 would pause the development-facing obligations of all three.

The costs are not abstract. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, aggregate results), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, 34% of surveyed startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months, and developers reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees assigned to SB 53 and RAISE compliance in parallel. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups. Every dollar spent conforming the same product to a third definition is a dollar not spent on research.

We ask that Sec. 121 preemption be made permanent. If a sunset is unavoidable, extend the window and structure reauthorization so a clean federal standard is in place before any lapse. Note that Secs. 111 and 112 also expire after three years; a synchronized sunset would leave the country with no federal standard, no preemption and the same patchwork on the other side, plus three years of transition costs.

**2. Fix the incident-reporting provision: Sec. 111(g), definition in Sec. 101**

As drafted, Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt to receive the reports, and violations can draw civil fines of up to $1 million per day. We oppose the provision as drafted, for three reasons.

First, the definition is unbounded. Section 101 defines a critical safety incident to include unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, "a failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," and "loss of control" of a model. The first category is a genuine security event. The second and third are not: a safety filter that misfires, or output that behaves unexpectedly, becomes a federal reportable event regardless of whether anyone was harmed.

Second, the reports are exposed. An incident report under this provision will describe weight thefts, security gaps and response plans, which is among the most sensitive information a developer holds. Nothing in the draft protects that material from disclosure once it reaches a federal agency.

Third, the penalties are unbalanced. A fine of up to $1 million per day with no safe harbor punishes the act of reporting and will chill exactly the disclosure the sponsors want.

Four changes: (1) narrow the Sec. 101 definition to incidents causing, or creating a credible imminent risk of, death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption; (2) hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject any drift toward the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois; (3) require confidential handling and a Freedom of Information Act exemption for incident reports; and (4) add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, with penalties reserved for knowing concealment. Our surveyed developers put the median one-time cost of standing up a reporting function at $310,000; a narrow definition keeps that function pointed at real events rather than paperwork.

**3. Codify CAISI, and keep its standards voluntary: Sec. 102**

Section 102 formally establishes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, charged with voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, evaluation of AI systems, monitoring of AI progress, synthetic content detection and administration of the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime. It authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, against a current appropriation of roughly $15 million, and grants special hiring authority for technical experts.

We support the codification. A permanent federal home for standards work, able to compete for technical talent, is a win for the whole ecosystem. The voluntary model is also working: in May 2026, CAISI announced pre-deployment evaluation agreements with three leading U.S. labs, extending the model of the 2024 agreements. That is the right template. Voluntary standards move faster, draw deeper industry participation and travel further internationally than mandates.

Two requests. Keep CAISI's testing and evaluation role voluntary: ACIA opposes any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, in this bill or a manager's amendment, and asks that nothing in the Sec. 112 verification regime operate as a government gate on deployment. And keep any CAISI fees cost-based. ACIA takes no position on the funding level itself.

**4. Keep the framework and audit obligations light-touch: Secs. 111 and 112**

Sections 111 and 112 require large frontier developers to publish and annually update a frontier AI framework, and to retain a CAISI-licensed IVO for audits at least semi-annually, including an assessment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation." These are real costs: our surveyed large developers report a median $1.4 million per year to maintain a published framework.

Two requests. Tie these obligations to demonstrated harms. The organizing concept of Subtitle B is "catastrophic risk," and assessments of hypothetical scenarios remain speculative. Speculation is not a sound basis for binding obligations, enforcement referrals or audits that second-guess a developer's risk judgment. Keep the regime risk-based: IVO audits should verify compliance with a developer's own published framework rather than adjudicate what a model might someday do. And preserve the Sec. 111(e) redaction rights for trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety and national security. We support the three-year sunset on both sections as a backstop, and repeat our request that a clean federal standard be in place before any lapse.

**5. Provisions we support without reservation**

ACIA supports the draft's buildout provisions: AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and NSF; codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource; international standards work that keeps the People's Republic of China out of U.S.-led coalitions; support for open-source software security; and the Sec. 122 GAO review of federal statutes and regulations that burden AI infrastructure, including energy. The Sec. 131 provisions raising maximum fines for AI-facilitated fraud, from $1 million to $2 million, are well aimed at demonstrated harms. Title II's workforce data provisions are a service: better data on AI's labor effects beats guessing.

**Closing**

America will win the AI race the way it has won every technology race: by building faster than anyone else. A 50-state patchwork taxes that speed and advantages the largest incumbents, who can absorb the overhead and would happily absorb the market share of those who cannot. GAAIA gets the big question right. Make the standard durable, keep it light-touch and risk-based, point it at demonstrated harms rather than speculative scenarios, and introduce it.

ACIA stands ready to work with both your offices and the Energy and Commerce Committee. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, at [email] or [phone]. Thank you for your bipartisan leadership.

Sincerely,

[Draft. ACIA-POL-2026-117. Prepared for sign-off by the President & CEO. Do not transmit.]

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[street address]
Washington, DC [zip]

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the bipartisan discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) on June 4 and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the chips and the data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI.

We support the draft's core. One national standard beats 50 state regimes, and a federal standard serves the country best when it is light-touch, risk-based and pointed at demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones. Our requests, in order:

1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption permanent, or extend it so a clean federal standard is in place before any sunset.
2. Narrow the Sec. 101 definition of "critical safety incident," hold the 15-day reporting window, add confidentiality and a safe harbor.
3. Codify CAISI (Sec. 102) and keep its standards and testing voluntary.
4. Keep the Sec. 111 and 112 obligations risk-based and tied to demonstrated harms.
5. Preserve the buildout provisions across Titles I through IV.

**1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption durable**

[para on scope] Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. The draft's carve-outs are well judged: states keep their civil rights, labor, copyright and consumer privacy laws, and consumers keep their day in court. Development is different. Frontier development is national by nature; a model trained in one state ships to all 50 on day one and cannot be re-papered for each of them.

[para on patchwork] The state layer is thickening fast. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour incident clock. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, signed July 6, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with its own 72-hour clock. Three frontier regimes in under a year, each with different definitions and thresholds. By most readings, Sec. 121 would pause the development-facing obligations of all three.

[para on costs] The costs are not abstract. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported in aggregate), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34% of surveyed startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers subject to both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, and every dollar spent conforming the same product to a third definition is a dollar not spent on research.

[ask] We ask that Sec. 121 be made permanent. That is consistent with the White House's March national AI policy framework, which called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. If a sunset is unavoidable, extend the window and structure reauthorization so a clean federal standard is in place before any lapse. Note that Secs. 111 and 112 also expire after three years. A synchronized sunset is the worst outcome: no federal standard, no preemption, and the same patchwork waiting on the other side, plus three years of transition costs on the way through.

**2. Fix incident reporting: Sec. 111(g) and the Sec. 101 definition**

As drafted, Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt to receive the reports, and violations can draw civil fines of up to $1 million per day. ACIA opposes the provision as drafted, for three reasons.

First, the definition is unbounded. Section 101 sweeps in unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, any "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," and "loss of control" of a model. The first is a genuine security event. The second and third are not: a safety filter that misfires, or output that behaves unexpectedly, becomes a federal reportable event regardless of whether anyone was harmed.

Second, the reports are exposed. A report under this provision will describe weight thefts, security gaps and response plans, among the most sensitive information a developer holds, and nothing in the draft protects it from disclosure once it reaches an agency.

Third, the penalties are unbalanced. A fine of up to $1 million per day with no safe harbor punishes the act of reporting and will chill exactly the disclosure the sponsors want.

Four changes. Narrow the definition to incidents causing, or creating a credible imminent risk of, death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption. Hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject any drift toward the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois, which assume investigation is complete at discovery. Require confidential handling and a Freedom of Information Act exemption for incident reports. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, with penalties reserved for knowing concealment. Our surveyed developers put the median one-time cost of standing up a reporting function at $310,000; a narrow definition keeps that function pointed at real events rather than paperwork.

**3. Codify CAISI, and keep its standards voluntary: Sec. 102**

Section 102 formally establishes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, charged with developing voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, evaluating AI systems, monitoring AI progress, supporting synthetic content detection and administering the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime. It authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, against a current appropriation of roughly $15 million, and grants special hiring authority for technical experts.

We support the codification. A permanent federal home for standards work, able to compete for technical talent, is a win for the whole ecosystem. The voluntary model is also working. In May 2026, CAISI announced pre-deployment evaluation agreements with three leading U.S. labs, extending the cooperation begun in 2024. That is the right template: voluntary standards move faster, draw deeper industry participation and travel further internationally than mandates.

Two requests. Keep CAISI's testing and evaluation role voluntary. ACIA opposes any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, in this bill or in a manager's amendment, and asks that nothing in the Sec. 112 verification regime operate as a government gate on deployment. Keep any CAISI fees cost-based. ACIA takes no position on the funding level itself; that is a question for the appropriators.

**4. Keep the framework and audit obligations light-touch: Secs. 111 and 112**

Sections 111 and 112 require large frontier developers to publish and annually update a frontier AI framework, and to retain a CAISI-licensed IVO for audits at least semi-annually, including an assessment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation." These are real costs. Our surveyed large developers report a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published framework.

Two requests. Tie these obligations to demonstrated harms. The organizing concept of Subtitle B is "catastrophic risk," and assessments of hypothetical scenarios are, by nature, speculative. Speculation is not a sound basis for binding obligations, for enforcement referrals, or for audits that second-guess a developer's risk judgment. Keep the regime risk-based: IVO audits should verify compliance with a developer's own published framework rather than adjudicate what a model might someday do. And preserve the Sec. 111(e) redaction rights for trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety and national security. We support the three-year sunset on both sections as a backstop, and repeat that a clean federal standard should be in place before any lapse.

**5. Provisions we support without reservation**

ACIA supports the draft's buildout provisions: AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and the National Science Foundation; codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource; international standards work that keeps the People's Republic of China out of U.S.-led coalitions; support for open-source software security; and the Sec. 122 GAO review of federal statutes and regulations that burden AI infrastructure, including energy. The Sec. 131 provisions raising maximum fines for AI-facilitated fraud, from $1 million to $2 million, are well aimed at demonstrated harms. The Sec. 113 whistleblower protections are worth keeping: real protections for workers who surface actual violations complement the safe harbor we have requested. Title II's workforce data provisions are a service, because better data on AI's labor effects beats guessing.

**Closing**

America will win the AI race the way it has won every technology race: by building faster than anyone else. A 50-state patchwork taxes that speed and advantages the largest incumbents, who can absorb the overhead and would happily absorb the market share of those who cannot. GAAIA gets the big question right. Make the standard durable, keep it light-touch and risk-based, point it at demonstrated harms rather than speculative scenarios, and introduce it.

ACIA stands ready to work with both of your offices and with the Energy and Commerce Committee. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, at [email] or [phone]. Thank you for your bipartisan leadership on a difficult file.

Sincerely,

Grant Holloway
President & Chief Executive Officer
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC
---

## The problem
Frontier developers face a fast-growing patchwork. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour incident clock. # Staff QA: anticipated questions

**1. Majority Energy and Commerce staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

We support preemption because one national standard beats 50 state regimes. Our objection to Sec. 111 incident reporting is the definition and the exposure, not the timeline. As drafted, a "critical safety incident" includes any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures or "loss of control," so a misfiring safety filter becomes a federal report. Reports reach CAISI, with state attorneys general able to opt in, without confidentiality or a FOIA exemption, and violations can draw fines of $1 million per day with no safe harbor. Note the draft's 15-day window already matches SB 53; we ask the committee to hold that line against the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois. function.arguments:
{"content": "[Draft. ACIA-POL-2026-117. Prepared for sign-off by the President & CEO. Not for transmission.]

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[street address]
Washington, DC [zip]

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the bipartisan discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) on June 4, and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the chips and the data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI.

We support the draft's core. One national standard beats 50 state regimes, and a federal standard serves the country best when it is light-touch, risk-based and pointed at demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones. Our requests, in order:

1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption permanent, or extend it so a clean federal standard is in place before any sunset.
2. Narrow the Sec. 101 definition of "critical safety incident," hold the 15-day reporting window, and add confidentiality and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
3. Codify CAISI (Sec. 102) and keep its standards and testing voluntary.
4. Keep the Sec. 111 and Sec. 112 obligations risk-based and tied to demonstrated harms.
5. Preserve the buildout provisions across Titles I through IV.

**1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption durable**

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. The draft's carve-outs are well judged: states keep their civil rights, labor, copyright and consumer privacy laws, and consumers keep their day in court. Development is different. Frontier development is national by nature. A model trained in one state ships to all 50 on day one, and it cannot be re-papered for each of them.

The state layer is thickening fast. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour incident clock. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, signed July 6, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with its own 72-hour clock. Three frontier regimes in under a year, each with different definitions and thresholds. By most readings, Sec. 121 would pause the development-facing obligations of all three.

The costs are not abstract. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported in aggregate), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34% of surveyed startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers subject to both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, and every dollar spent conforming the same product to a third definition is a dollar not spent on research.

We ask that Sec. 121 be made permanent. That is consistent with the White House's March national AI policy framework, which called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. If a sunset is unavoidable, extend the window and structure reauthorization so a clean federal standard is in place before any lapse. Note that Secs. 111 and 112 also expire after three years. A synchronized sunset is the worst outcome: no federal standard, no preemption, and the same patchwork waiting on the other side, with three years of transition costs on the way through.

**2. Fix incident reporting: Sec. 111(g) and the Sec. 101 definition**

As drafted, Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt to receive the reports, and violations can draw civil fines of up to $1 million per day. ACIA opposes the provision as drafted, for three reasons.

First, the definition is unbounded. Section 101 sweeps in unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, any "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," and "loss of control" of a model. The first is a genuine security event. The second and third are not. A safety filter that misfires, or output that behaves unexpectedly, becomes a federal reportable event regardless of whether anyone was harmed.

Second, the reports are exposed. A report under this provision will describe weight thefts, security gaps and response plans, among the most sensitive information a developer holds, and nothing in the draft protects it from disclosure once it reaches an agency.

Third, the penalties are unbalanced. A fine of up to $1 million per day, with no safe harbor, punishes the act of reporting and will chill exactly the disclosure the sponsors want.

Note the reach. The reporting duty applies to every frontier developer, Sec. 101's tier above $50 million in gross revenue, while the framework and audit obligations sit with large frontier developers, the tier above $500 million. That tiering is sensible, and the reporting duty belongs in the same tier.

Five changes. Narrow the definition to incidents causing, or creating a credible imminent risk of, death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption. Hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject any drift toward the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois, which presume investigation is complete at discovery. Require confidential handling and a Freedom of Information Act exemption for incident reports. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, with penalties reserved for knowing concealment. And place the reporting duty with Subtitle B's other heavy obligations, in the large frontier developer tier. Our surveyed developers put the median one-time cost of standing up a reporting function at $310,000. A narrow definition keeps that function pointed at real events rather than paperwork.

**3. Codify CAISI, and keep its standards voluntary: Sec. 102**

Section 102 formally establishes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, charged with developing voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, evaluating AI systems, monitoring AI progress, supporting synthetic content detection and administering the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime. It authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, against a current appropriation of roughly $15 million, and grants special hiring authority for technical experts.

We support the codification. A permanent federal home for standards work, able to compete for technical talent, is a win for the whole ecosystem. The voluntary model is also working. In May 2026, CAISI announced pre-deployment evaluation agreements with three leading U.S. labs, extending the cooperation begun in 2024. That is the right template. Voluntary standards move faster, draw deeper industry participation and travel further internationally than mandates.

Two requests. Keep CAISI's testing and evaluation role voluntary. ACIA opposes any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, in this bill or in a manager's amendment, and asks that nothing in the Sec. 112 verification regime operate as a government gate on deployment. Keep any CAISI fees cost-based. ACIA takes no position on the funding level itself; that is a question for the appropriators.

**4. Keep the framework and audit obligations light-touch: Secs. 111 and 112**

Sections 111 and 112 require large frontier developers to publish and update at least annually a frontier AI framework, and to retain a CAISI-licensed IVO for audits at least semi-annually, including an assessment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation." These are real costs. Our surveyed large developers report a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published framework.

Two requests. Tie these obligations to demonstrated harms. The organizing concept of Subtitle B is "catastrophic risk," and assessments of hypothetical scenarios are, by their nature, speculative. Speculation is not a sound basis for binding obligations, for enforcement referrals, or for audits that second-guess a developer's risk judgment. Keep the regime risk-based: IVO audits should verify compliance with a developer's own published framework rather than adjudicate what a model might someday do. Preserve the Sec. 111(e) redaction rights for trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety and national security. We support the three-year sunset on both sections as a backstop, and repeat that a clean federal standard should be in place before any lapse.

**5. Provisions we support without reservation**

ACIA supports the draft's buildout provisions: AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and the National Science Foundation; codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource; international standards work that keeps the People's Republic of China out of U.S.-led coalitions; support for open-source software security; and the Sec. 122 GAO review of federal statutes and regulations that burden AI infrastructure, including energy. The Sec. 131 provisions raising maximum fines for AI-facilitated fraud, from $1 million to $2 million, are well aimed at demonstrated harms. The Sec. 113 whistleblower protections are worth keeping: real protection for workers who surface actual violations complements the safe harbor we have requested. Title II's workforce data provisions are a service, because better data on AI's labor effects beats guessing.

**Closing**

America will win the AI race the way it has won every technology race: by building faster than anyone else. A 50-state patchwork taxes that speed and advantages the largest incumbents, who can absorb the overhead and would happily absorb the market share of those who cannot. GAAIA gets the big question right. It regulates the development of frontier systems rather than every use of AI, it puts its heaviest duties on the largest developers, and it preserves state authority where states govern best. Make the standard durable, keep it light-touch and risk-based, point it at demonstrated harms rather than speculative scenarios, and introduce it.

ACIA stands ready to work with both of your offices and with the Energy and Commerce Committee. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, at [email] or [phone]. Thank you for your bipartisan leadership on a difficult file.

Sincerely,

Grant Holloway
President & Chief Executive Officer
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC", "path": "/workspace/out/comment_letter_GAAIA.md"}
