# ACIA asks on the GAAIA discussion draft, by section

| Draft provision | Our position | Requested change | One-line rationale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sec. 121.** Preemption of state/local laws specifically regulating AI model development; three-year sunset; carve-outs for use/deployment, general applicability and common-law remedies | Support as scoped | Make preemption permanent; at minimum, extend it so a clean federal standard is in place before any sunset | One national standard beats 50 state regimes, and a sunset invites 50 new ones. |
| **Sec. 101.** Definitions: frontier model by compute threshold; frontier developer ($50M+ revenue); large frontier developer ($500M+ revenue) | Support the tiering, amend one term | Keep the large frontier developer tier as the home for the heaviest duties; align the incident-reporting duty with it | Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, so duties should track capacity. |
| **Sec. 101, "critical safety incident."** Includes model weight access, modification or exfiltration; any failure of risk-mitigation measures; "loss of control" | Oppose as drafted | Narrow to incidents causing, or creating a credible imminent risk of, death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption | Regulate demonstrated harms; as drafted, a misfiring safety filter becomes a federal report. |
| **Sec. 111(g).** Incident reports to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery; 24 hours to law enforcement for imminent risk of death or serious injury; state attorneys general may opt in | Support the window, oppose the package | Hold the 15-day window (SB 53's calibration) and reject any drift to 72-hour clocks (NY RAISE, Illinois SB 315) | Fifteen days matches California and leaves room to investigate before reporting. |
| **Sec. 111(g) handling and penalties.** Reports to an agency without confidentiality protections; civil fines up to $1 million per day; no safe harbor | Oppose as drafted | Confidential handling with a FOIA exemption; safe harbor for good-faith reporters; penalties reserved for knowing concealment | Reports will describe weight thefts and security gaps, and fining reporters chills disclosure. |
| **Sec. 111(a), (c)-(e).** Published frontier AI framework, annual updates, pre-deployment transparency reports, redaction rights | Support with changes | Preserve redaction rights (Sec. 111(e)) and keep the report contents factual, current and tied to real risks | Transparency works when it describes what a model does, not what it might someday do. |
| **Sec. 102.** Codifies CAISI at Commerce: voluntary guidelines and standards, evaluation, monitoring, synthetic content detection, IVO licensing; $100M/year, FY2027-2029; special hiring authority | Support codification; no position on funding | Keep testing and evaluation voluntary; no mandatory pre-deployment testing authority; keep fees cost-based | Voluntary standards move faster and travel further than mandates. |
| **Sec. 112.** CAISI-licensed IVO audits at least semi-annually; adequacy findings on "catastrophic-risk mitigation"; three-year sunset | Support with changes | Audits verify compliance with the developer's own published framework, not hypothetical scenarios; keep the sunset with a clean successor standard in place first | Speculation is not a sound basis for an enforcement referral. |
| **Sec. 113.** Whistleblower protections; anti-retaliation; remedies incl. double back pay | Support | None; keep as drafted | Workers who surface actual violations complement a good-faith safe harbor. |
| **Sec. 122.** GAO review of federal statutes and regulations burdening AI innovation and infrastructure, incl. energy | Support | None; use the findings | Better data on federal barriers beats guessing. |
| **Sec. 131.** Raises maximum fines in federal fraud statutes, from $1 million to $2 million, and adds penalties when AI is used | Support | None | Enforcement aimed at demonstrated harms is the right model. |
| **Title II.** Workforce and labor-market data provisions | Support | None | Better data on AI's labor effects beats guessing. |
| **Title IV.** AI testbeds (DOE, NIST, NSF), NAIRR codification, international standards excluding the PRC; open-source security support | Support | Fund testbeds and NAIRR at authorized levels | Compute buildout and R&D are how the United States stays ahead. |

**Aggregate survey basis (ACIA, Aug. 2026, n=86):** 61% cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance issue; 34% of surveyed startups delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months; median 6.5 FTEs for parallel SB 53 and RAISE compliance; median $310,000 one-time cost to stand up an incident-reporting function; median $1.4 million per year to maintain a published framework (developers above $500 million revenue).

[Draft. ACIA-POL-2026-117. Prepared for sign-off by the President & CEO. Not for transmission.]

**AMERICAN COMPUTE & INNOVATION ALLIANCE**
[street address]
Washington, DC [zip]

October 28, 2026

The Honorable Jay Obernolte
The Honorable Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Via email: GAAIA@mail.house.gov

RE: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026

Dear Representatives Obernolte and Trahan:

Thank you for releasing the bipartisan discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act (GAAIA) on June 4, and for taking stakeholder comment before introduction. The American Compute & Innovation Alliance (ACIA) is a Washington, DC coalition of roughly 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, semiconductor startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the chips and the data centers that will determine whether the United States leads the world in AI.

We support the draft's core. One national standard beats 50 state regimes, and a federal standard serves the country best when it is light-touch, risk-based and pointed at demonstrated harms rather than speculative ones. Our requests, in order:

1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption permanent, or extend it so a clean federal standard is in place before any sunset.
2. Narrow the Sec. 101 definition of "critical safety incident," hold the 15-day reporting window, and add confidentiality and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters.
3. Codify CAISI (Sec. 102) and keep its standards and testing voluntary.
4. Keep the Sec. 111 and Sec. 112 obligations risk-based and tied to demonstrated harms.
5. Preserve the buildout provisions across Titles I through IV.

**1. Make the Sec. 121 preemption durable**

Section 121 would preempt state and local laws that specifically regulate the development of AI models, while preserving laws of general applicability, common-law remedies and state authority over use and deployment. The draft's carve-outs are well judged: states keep their civil rights, labor, copyright and consumer privacy laws, and consumers keep their day in court. Development is different. Frontier development is national by nature. A model trained in one state ships to all 50 on day one, and it cannot be re-papered for each of them.

The state layer is thickening fast. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act, finalized by chapter amendment on March 27, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour incident clock. Illinois' Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, signed July 6, 2026, takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with its own 72-hour clock. Three frontier regimes in under a year, each with different definitions and thresholds. By most readings, Sec. 121 would pause the development-facing obligations of all three.

The costs are not abstract. In our August 2026 member survey (86 responding members, reported in aggregate), 61% cited conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem, and 34% of surveyed startups had delayed a launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Developers subject to both SB 53 and the RAISE Act reported a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups, and every dollar spent conforming the same product to a third definition is a dollar not spent on research.

We ask that Sec. 121 be made permanent. That is consistent with the White House's March national AI policy framework, which called on Congress to preempt state AI laws that impose undue burdens. If a sunset is unavoidable, extend the window and structure reauthorization so a clean federal standard is in place before any lapse. Note that Secs. 111 and 112 also expire after three years. A synchronized sunset is the worst outcome: no federal standard, no preemption, and the same patchwork waiting on the other side, with three years of transition costs on the way through.

**2. Fix incident reporting: Sec. 111(g) and the Sec. 101 definition**

As drafted, Sec. 111 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the CAISI Director within 15 days of discovery, and to law enforcement within 24 hours where an incident poses an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt to receive the reports, and violations can draw civil fines of up to $1 million per day. ACIA opposes the provision as drafted, for three reasons.

First, the definition is unbounded. Section 101 sweeps in unauthorized access to, modification of or exfiltration of model weights, any "failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures," and "loss of control" of a model. The first is a genuine security event. The second and third are not. A safety filter that misfires, or output that behaves unexpectedly, becomes a federal reportable event regardless of whether anyone was harmed.

Second, the reports are exposed. A report under this provision will describe weight thefts, security gaps and response plans, among the most sensitive information a developer holds, and nothing in the draft protects it from disclosure once it reaches an agency.

Third, the penalties are unbalanced. A fine of up to $1 million per day, with no safe harbor, punishes the act of reporting and will chill exactly the disclosure the sponsors want.

Note the reach. The reporting duty applies to every frontier developer, Sec. 101's tier above $50 million in gross revenue, while the framework and audit obligations sit with large frontier developers, the tier above $500 million. That tiering is sensible, and the reporting duty belongs in the same tier.

Five changes. Narrow the definition to incidents causing, or creating a credible imminent risk of, death, serious injury, major property damage or critical infrastructure disruption. Hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject any drift toward the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois, which presume investigation is complete at discovery. Require confidential handling and a Freedom of Information Act exemption for incident reports. Add a safe harbor for good-faith reporters, with penalties reserved for knowing concealment. And place the reporting duty with Subtitle B's other heavy obligations, in the large frontier developer tier. Our surveyed developers put the median one-time cost of standing up a reporting function at $310,000. A narrow definition keeps that function pointed at real events rather than paperwork.

**3. Codify CAISI, and keep its standards voluntary: Sec. 102**

Section 102 formally establishes the Center for AI Standards and Innovation at the Department of Commerce under a Secretary-appointed Director, charged with developing voluntary guidelines, best practices and standards for AI security, evaluating AI systems, monitoring AI progress, supporting synthetic content detection and administering the independent verification organization (IVO) licensing regime. It authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029, against a current appropriation of roughly $15 million, and grants special hiring authority for technical experts.

We support the codification. A permanent federal home for standards work, able to compete for technical talent, is a win for the whole ecosystem. The voluntary model is also working. In May 2026, CAISI announced pre-deployment evaluation agreements with three leading U.S. labs, extending the cooperation begun in 2024. That is the right template. Voluntary standards move faster, draw deeper industry participation and travel further internationally than mandates.

Two requests. Keep CAISI's testing and evaluation role voluntary. ACIA opposes any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority, in this bill or in a manager's amendment, and asks that nothing in the Sec. 112 verification regime operate as a government gate on deployment. Keep any CAISI fees cost-based. ACIA takes no position on the funding level itself; that is a question for the appropriators.

**4. Keep the framework and audit obligations light-touch: Secs. 111 and 112**

Sections 111 and 112 require large frontier developers to publish and update at least annually a frontier AI framework, and to retain a CAISI-licensed IVO for audits at least semi-annually, including an assessment of whether the framework achieves "acceptable levels of catastrophic-risk mitigation." These are real costs. Our surveyed large developers report a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published framework.

Two requests. Tie these obligations to demonstrated harms. The organizing concept of Subtitle B is "catastrophic risk," and assessments of hypothetical scenarios are, by their nature, speculative. Speculation is not a sound basis for binding obligations, for enforcement referrals, or for audits that second-guess a developer's risk judgment. Keep the regime risk-based: IVO audits should verify compliance with a developer's own published framework rather than adjudicate what a model might someday do. Preserve the Sec. 111(e) redaction rights for trade secrets, cybersecurity, public safety and national security. We support the three-year sunset on both sections as a backstop, and repeat that a clean federal standard should be in place before any lapse.

**5. Provisions we support without reservation**

ACIA supports the draft's buildout provisions: AI testbeds at the Department of Energy, NIST and the National Science Foundation; codification of the National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource; international standards work that keeps the People's Republic of China out of U.S.-led coalitions; support for open-source software security; and the Sec. 122 GAO review of federal statutes and regulations that burden AI infrastructure, including energy. The Sec. 131 provisions raising maximum fines in the federal fraud statutes, from $1 million to $2 million, and adding penalties when AI is used are well aimed at demonstrated harms. The Sec. 113 whistleblower protections are worth keeping: real protection for workers who surface actual violations complements the safe harbor we have requested. Title II's workforce data provisions are a service, because better data on AI's labor effects beats guessing.

**Closing**

America will win the AI race the way it has won every technology race: by building faster than anyone else. A 50-state patchwork taxes that speed and advantages the largest incumbents, who can absorb the overhead and would happily absorb the market share of those who cannot. GAAIA gets the big question right. It regulates the development of frontier systems rather than every use of AI, it puts its heaviest duties on the largest developers, and it preserves state authority where states govern best. Make the standard durable, keep it light-touch and risk-based, point it at demonstrated harms rather than speculative scenarios, and introduce it.

ACIA stands ready to work with both of your offices and with the Energy and Commerce Committee. Please contact Tessa Marchetti, our vice president for policy, at [email] or [phone]. Thank you for your bipartisan leadership on a difficult file.

Sincerely,

Grant Holloway
President & Chief Executive Officer
American Compute & Innovation Alliance
Washington, DC

# One national standard for frontier AI: back GAAIA, fix it in four places

## Who we are
ACIA is a Washington, DC coalition of about 140 AI developers, cloud and data center operators, chip startups and venture firms. Our members build the models, the chips and the data centers behind U.S. AI leadership.

## The problem
Frontier developers face a fast-growing patchwork. California's SB 53 took effect Jan. 1, 2026. New York's RAISE Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with a 72-hour incident clock. Illinois' AI Safety Measures Act takes effect Jan. 1, 2027 with its own 72-hour clock. Three regimes in under a year, each with different definitions and thresholds.

The costs are real. In ACIA's August 2026 survey: 61% of members cite conflicting state definitions as their top compliance problem; 34% of surveyed startups delayed a launch in California or New York in the past year; developers subject to both SB 53 and RAISE report a median of 6.5 full-time employees for parallel compliance. Compliance costs fall hardest on startups.

## Our position
Support the draft's core. One national standard beats 50 state regimes. Keep it light-touch, risk-based and pointed at demonstrated harms. Speculative catastrophic-risk scenarios are not a basis for binding obligations.

## Four asks
1. **Make Sec. 121 preemption durable.** Make it permanent. At minimum, extend it so a clean federal standard is in place before any sunset. Secs. 111 and 112 also lapse after three years; a synchronized sunset hands the field back to the states.
2. **Fix incident reporting (Sec. 111(g), definition in Sec. 101).** Narrow "critical safety incident" to actual or credible imminent serious harm. Hold the 15-day window, which matches SB 53, and reject 72-hour clocks. Add confidential handling, a FOIA exemption and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters. Fines as drafted reach $1 million per day.
3. **Keep CAISI voluntary (Sec. 102).** We support codifying CAISI at Commerce ($100 million per year for fiscal 2027 through 2029) and its voluntary standards, evaluation and IVO licensing roles. Oppose any mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. No position on the funding level.
4. **Protect the buildout.** Preserve AI testbeds, the NAIRR codification, international standards work that excludes China, open-source security support and the Sec. 122 GAO review, including energy burdens on AI infrastructure.

## Bottom line
America wins the AI race by building. A 50-state patchwork taxes that speed and advantages the largest incumbents. Pass one national standard, aim it at demonstrated harms, and make it last.

Contact: Tessa Marchetti, VP Policy, ACIA, [email], [phone].

[Draft. ACIA-POL-2026-117. Answers for anticipated staffer questions, Sept. 2026 Hill meetings. Max 120 words each.]

# Staff QA: anticipated questions

**1. Majority Energy and Commerce staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

We support preemption because one national standard beats 50 state regimes. Our objection to Sec. 111 incident reporting is the definition and the exposure, not the timeline. As drafted, a "critical safety incident" includes any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures or "loss of control," so a misfiring safety filter becomes a federal report. Reports reach CAISI, where state attorneys general may opt in, with no confidentiality protection or FOIA exemption, and violations can draw fines of $1 million per day with no safe harbor. The draft's 15-day window already matches SB 53; we ask the committee to hold that line against the 72-hour clocks in New York and Illinois. With those fixes we can support it.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Several in this draft. We accept a published frontier AI framework and pre-deployment transparency reports for large frontier developers. We support codifying CAISI at Commerce with voluntary standards, evaluation, monitoring and IVO licensing. We would accept incident reporting to CAISI within the 15-day window already in the draft, with a narrow definition tied to actual or credible imminent serious harm, confidential handling and a safe harbor for good-faith reporters. We would also accept periodic IVO audits that verify compliance with a developer's own published framework. What we cannot accept are binding obligations built on speculative catastrophic-risk scenarios. Point the duties at demonstrated harms and we are at the table.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent: what is the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. That is our board-approved position. If permanence is not achievable this Congress, the fallback is an extension structured so a clean federal standard is in place before any sunset. Two details matter. Secs. 111 and 112 also expire after three years, so a synchronized lapse would leave no federal standard and no preemption, which is today's patchwork plus three years of transition costs. And a three-year window invites state legislatures to queue replacement bills for the day it expires. Our members are already complying with SB 53 and preparing for RAISE and Illinois SB 315. Durability is the whole value of preemption.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million per year. What is your view on the funding level?"**

ACIA takes no position on the dollar figure. That is a board-approved posture, and the level is an appropriations question for your committee. What we care about is what the money buys. We support codifying CAISI at Commerce, the special hiring authority for technical experts, and a voluntary standards, evaluation and monitoring mission. We would oppose using any funding to build mandatory pre-deployment testing authority. For context, CAISI's current appropriation is roughly $15 million, so the draft is a tenfold step up. Fund the voluntary mission at a level that lets CAISI compete for technical talent, and that is money well spent.
